title: Glomerular Disease: Nephritic and Nephrotic Syndromes, Biopsy Safety and Complication Surveillance
html:
Glomeruli are the kidney's microscopic filters. Injury may allow blood or protein to pass into urine and may reduce filtration, raise blood pressure, and cause edema. The RN recognizes patterns rather than treating a urine color or protein result as a diagnosis, protects clients during evaluation and kidney biopsy, and watches for rapid kidney decline, fluid overload, infection, and thrombosis.

Learning goals

  • Compare nephritic and nephrotic patterns while recognizing that they can overlap.
  • Connect hematuria, proteinuria, albumin, weight, urine output, blood pressure, and creatinine trends.
  • Identify red flags for rapidly progressive glomerular injury and pulmonary–renal disease.
  • Explain the purpose and nursing safety checks for a kidney biopsy.
  • Monitor edema, infection, clotting, medication effects, and follow-up response.

Two useful patterns, not two final diagnoses

A nephritic pattern emphasizes glomerular inflammation: blood in urine, often with protein, rising creatinine, reduced urine output, hypertension, and edema. Urine microscopy may show dysmorphic red cells or red-cell casts, which strongly support a glomerular source. A nephrotic pattern emphasizes substantial protein loss: heavy proteinuria, low serum albumin, edema, and often elevated blood lipids. Foamy urine can be a clue but is not diagnostic. A person may have features of both patterns.

Neither pattern names the cause. Possible causes include immune or inflammatory disease, diabetes, lupus, IgA nephropathy, membranous disease, minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, infection-related disease, medication-related injury, and other conditions. Treatments differ; do not assume every case needs steroids, antibiotics, or anticoagulation.

Remember the dominant clue
Nephritic: blood and inflammation with possible falling filtration. Nephrotic: large protein loss and low albumin with edema. Both can coexist, so report the full pattern.

Assess the trend and the person

Ask about onset and recurrence of red or cola-colored urine, foamy urine, facial or leg swelling, rapid weight gain, fatigue, infection symptoms, rash, joint pain, recent medicines, diabetes, hypertension, and family history. Assess blood pressure, pulse, oxygenation, work of breathing, edema distribution, skin integrity, daily weight, intake and output, and urine appearance. Evaluate creatinine and estimated GFR against baseline, urinalysis and microscopy, quantitative urine protein or albumin measurement, serum albumin, electrolytes, and ordered immune or infection studies.

Hematuria has many causes, including urinary infection, stones, tumors, and glomerular disease. Protein on a dipstick may need confirmation and quantification. A single normal creatinine does not rule out active glomerular damage, and a sudden rise in a client with CKD can be a new acute injury. Accurate measurement and timed trends are more useful than a reassuring isolated result.

Nephritic deterioration may be time-sensitive

Rapidly rising creatinine, falling urine output, severe hypertension, pulmonary edema, or an active urine sediment requires prompt nephrology evaluation. New hemoptysis or unexplained respiratory distress together with glomerular findings raises concern for a pulmonary–renal syndrome, such as anti-glomerular basement membrane disease or vasculitis. Protect the airway and oxygenation, escalate immediately, and prepare ordered studies; do not wait for the final biopsy report while the client deteriorates.

Check for hypertensive emergency symptoms, including severe headache, visual or neurologic change, chest pain, and dyspnea. Assess potassium and acid–base status as kidney function changes. Escalate unstable rhythm, severe hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, or shock using the emergency pathway. Do not interpret less urine as proof that the client needs a fluid bolus: inflammatory kidney injury may coexist with fluid overload.

Nephrotic complications extend beyond edema

Albumin loss reduces plasma oncotic pressure and contributes to fluid moving into tissues. Despite visible edema, the effective circulating volume can be low in some clients. Assess perfusion and lungs before adjusting fluids or diuretics. Track weight, swelling, skin breakdown, breathing, blood pressure, urine output, and electrolytes. Ordered sodium and fluid guidance should be individualized; overly aggressive diuresis may cause hypovolemia or kidney injury.

Nephrotic syndrome can increase the risk of venous thrombosis and infection. Sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, hypoxemia, or unilateral leg swelling needs urgent evaluation for thromboembolism. Fever or focal infection signs require prompt assessment, especially if the client receives immunosuppressive therapy. Anticoagulant prophylaxis is individualized to clotting and bleeding risk; it is not automatic for every proteinuric client.

Find the cause before choosing disease-specific therapy

Urine tests, blood studies, imaging, and often a kidney biopsy help establish the specific disease and whether injury is active or scarred. Supportive care may include blood-pressure control, reduction of proteinuria, edema management, cardiovascular risk reduction, and protection from nephrotoxins. Cause-specific therapy may include immunosuppression for selected disorders or treatment of an underlying infection or systemic disease. The RN verifies the actual plan, checks kidney dosing and interactions, watches for infection and metabolic adverse effects, and reinforces follow-up rather than generalizing one regimen to all glomerular disease.

Kidney biopsy: prevent and detect bleeding

Before a percutaneous kidney biopsy, confirm identification, the informed-consent process, the procedure and site, blood pressure, bleeding history, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs and supplements, ordered blood counts and coagulation tests, allergies, and baseline urine appearance and vital signs. Follow the procedural team's exact medication-hold and fasting instructions; do not independently stop prescribed therapy. Explain positioning, expected monitoring, and the need to report pain, dizziness, or heavy blood in urine.

After biopsy, follow ordered activity restriction and observe blood pressure, pulse, pain, puncture site, and urine for bleeding. Mild short-lived discomfort or a small amount of transient pink urine may occur, but dark red urine, clots, increasing flank pain, hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, or inability to void needs prompt assessment and escalation. A stable dressing does not exclude internal bleeding. Before discharge, verify the observation period and teach activity limits, warning signs, and where to seek help.

Evaluate treatment and support daily life

Response may be seen in reduced proteinuria, stable or improving kidney function, controlled blood pressure, less edema, better breathing and function, and no treatment complications. These do not always change together or immediately. Review home weight and blood-pressure tracking if ordered, medication adherence, nutrition with a renal dietitian, infection prevention, vaccination guidance, and scheduled urine and blood tests. Teach the client to report reduced urine, rapid swelling, breathlessness, fever, visible blood or clots in urine, and possible clot symptoms.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify hematuria, quantified proteinuria, albumin, creatinine and urine-output trends, edema, blood pressure, breathing, systemic symptoms, medicines, and biopsy status.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish nephritic from nephrotic predominance, consider overlapping disease, evaluate other causes of hematuria, and relate edema to both tissue and circulating volume.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Rapid kidney decline, pulmonary hemorrhage, severe hypertension, pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia, thromboembolism, infection, or post-biopsy bleeding requires urgent action.
  4. Generate solutions: Support airway and perfusion, obtain ordered urine and blood studies, arrange prompt nephrology assessment, protect skin and volume status, and prepare safe biopsy or cause-specific therapy.
  5. Take action: Communicate precise trends, follow procedure and emergency protocols, verify medication and bleeding risks, and monitor for infection or clotting.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Trend proteinuria, urine sediment, kidney function, blood pressure, weight, breathing, edema, pain, bleeding, treatment toxicity, and follow-up completion.

Clinical example

A client develops cola-colored urine, rising blood pressure, new edema, and creatinine that has increased rapidly from baseline. The RN confirms urine and laboratory trends, assesses breathing, potassium, urine output, and systemic symptoms, and contacts the nephrology team promptly. When the client also reports coughing blood, the RN recognizes possible pulmonary–renal disease and escalates immediately while supporting oxygenation. The cause is investigated with ordered tests and possibly biopsy; the RN does not assume that a single positive urine test identifies the disease.

Original educational synthesis. Glomerular diagnosis, biopsy decisions and precautions, fluid and blood-pressure treatment, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, and emergency management require current client data, authorized orders, local protocols, specialist assessment, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official NIDDK or KDIGO product.
